The Executive Centre expands in Singapore and Manila, adding 75,000 sq ft to its Southeast Asia footprint
article:
Flexible workspace provider The Executive Centre has expanded with three new workspaces across Singapore and the Philippines, adding 75,000 sq ft to its Southeast Asia footprint.

In Singapore, it opened a 23,500 sq ft location on Level 40 of IOI Central Boulevard Towers in Marina Bay, offering over 300 workstations. The Executive Operator already operates approximately 20,000 sq ft of workspaces on Level 32, which officially opened early this year.

It also opened a 21,800 sq ft centre with 300 workstations at Level 34 of Frasers Tower , a Grade A office building on Cecil Street. The new space adds to The Executive Centre’s existing operations at Frasers Tower, spanning about 20,500 sq ft on Level 17.

In the Philippines, the group opened a 30,000 sq ft location at Six/Neo in Bonifacio Global City in Manila.

The three new locations bring the The Executive Centre’s Southeast Asia portfolio to over 560,000 sq ft.

The expansion comes as businesses continue to reassess their workplace strategies amid changing occupier requirements and constrained availability of premium space, the company said in a Nov 24 release. It added that enterprise clients no longer view flexible workspace as a temporary stopgap, but as a core real estate strategy.

Businesses are increasingly seeking workplaces that combine prime locations, quality, hospitality, and the ability to adapt as requirements change, said Yvonne Lim, regional managing director at The Executive Centre.

“With these three new centres, we are strengthening our Southeast Asia network while giving enterprises greater choice and access to premium workspace solutions that can support both their immediate needs and long-term growth,” she added.

title: More Singapore occupiers planning to increase office space; AI impact on demand still unclear: CBRE survey
article:
More companies in Singapore are expecting to expand their office space over the next three years, a CBRE survey has found.

The firm’s 2026 Asia Pacific (Apac) Office Occupier Survey , which surveyed 651 respondents across the region between May 27 and July 10, found that 50% are looking to grow their office footprint, up from 32% in the past three years, amid an increase in office attendance.

Singapore follows the same pattern, with 41% of the 18 Singapore respondents polled expecting to expand their office space over the next three years, up from 29% in the past three years. About 71% are targeting office space in CBD locations, while 76% prefer Grade A buildings.

The higher proportion points to “renewed confidence in the role of the office as a platform for growth”, said Tricia Song, CBRE’s head of research for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

“Compared with three years ago, a significantly higher proportion of companies are planning to expand their office footprint, supported by consistently strong workplace attendance and a clear preference for CBD locations and Grade A buildings," she added.

About 94% of Singapore respondents said their staff now attends the office at least three days per week, higher than the 75% indicated last year. Office attendance is now the highest since the pandemic, CBRE added.

Singapore’s office attendance rate outpaces the wider Apac region, with 88% of all survey respondents indicating staff spend at least three days in the office.

While optimisation of existing office space continues to be a priority for Apac occupiers, CBRE noted that utilisation is being balanced with the need to provide an attractive workplace experience.

While more companies have opted for unassigned seating over fixed desk arrangements, sharing ratios have largely plateaued at the 1 to 1.5 range, down from previously prevalent ratios exceeding two staff to one desk.

In addition, occupiers are leaning towards larger workstations, reversing a shrinkage of desk sizes observed in Apac in recent years. About 42% of the survey’s respondents indicated a preferred desk size of over 100 sq ft, higher than the 35% recorded in 2024.

In Singapore, 75% of respondents want to keep desk sharing ratios below 1:1.5, while 53% expect workstation size to be above 100 sq ft.

CBRE’s survey also highlighted that despite growing AI adoption, the impact on office demand remains unclear. Over half (56%) of respondents across Apac believe AI will have no meaningful impact on their office footprint or consider it too early to make an assessment.

In Singapore, that segment is even higher, at 65%. In addition, 24% of Singapore respondents believe more office space will be required due to AI adoption.

title: JustCo hits 60 operational centres, another 11 in the pipeline
article:
JustCo Holdings opened 10 new centres in the first nine months of 2026. This included centres in three new markets: India, Malaysia and the Philippines.

This brings its number of operational centres to 60, the Singapore Exchange -listed flexible workspace provider said in its latest business update, published on Nov 24.

The group’s blended occupancy for the first nine months stood at 79%. Centres that opened before 2026 have an occupancy of 84%, while centres that opened in 2026 have an occupancy of 23%.

JustCo Holdings, whose brands include JustCo, The Collective and The Boring Office, has a further pipeline of 11 centres set to open over the next 12 months, five of which are in Singapore.

They comprise a new floor at Central Plaza on Tiong Bahru Road, where the group already has an existing JustCo, along with new centres at The Octagon and Raffles City.

It is also slated to unveil the retail podium at JustCo Place , a co-working, co-living and retail development at 160 Orchard Road in December. The co-working component was completed in September, and is fully leased by Deloitte Singapore.

The co-living spaces, comprising 123 units that will be operated under a new Just At brand, will be ready next year.  The co-living units range from studios to three-bedroom spaces.

Despite the group’s ongoing expansions, JustCo Holdings’ cash balance stood at US$167 million (about $216 million) as of Sept 30, an increase from US$104 million as at Dec 31, 2025. It is also remains Cash ebitda positive, the group added.

title: 'AI talent war' to support rental demand for private housing: Realion
article:
The private residential rental market is expected to see steady demand in 2027, backed by AI-related expat talent seeking homes.

Total leasing volume for the private housing market is expected to range between 90,000 to 95,000 units next year, comparable to the 93,000 to 95,000 leases estimated for 2026, Realion (OrangeTee & ETC) Group said in a November research report.

It estimates private home rents to climb 3% to 4% next year, up from 2.5% to 3% in 2026.

Realion’s upbeat outlook for the private housing rental market comes amid an “AI talent war” that has driven up skilled professional compensation.

As the AI industry has seen a boom in investments, more high-net-worth individuals have emerged, resulting in a pool of “AI-elite, high-income tenants” entering the rental market, Realion said.

At the same time, rental housing supply is expected to increase in coming years, largely due to more HDB flats achieving their five-year minimum occupation period (MOP). Realion estimates almost 100,000 flats will reach their MOP between 2026 and 2030.

“The supply increase will impact both private and public markets, since many new flats offer desirable attributes, such as good connectivity and design features, that appeal to a wider audience,” the report added.

Private housing supply will also increase, with Realion projecting the number of new private homes completions to jump from around 7,783 units in 2026 to 8,858 units in 2027, excluding executive condos.

Despite the bump up in rental housing supply, Realion expects the AI-driven increase in the tenant pool, coupled with limited supply of prime residences, to support leasing demand for private homes next year.

On the other hand, rental demand for HDB flats, especially smaller units, could ease in 2027. “As the government continues to launch more BTO flats and speed up construction of existing ones, some local households or tenants may move from renting to owner-occupation, reducing the pool of local tenants,” Realion explained.

Another factor that may impact the rental market is the completion of the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link next year. The enhanced cross-border connectivity could prompt some tenants, especially those in the north, to relocate to Johor Bahru due to lower housing costs.

Realion is projecting HDB leasing volume of 32,000 to 35,000 in 2027, down from 36,000 to 38,000 in 2026. It anticipates HDB rents to move between -1% and 2% for next year.

title: Johor-Singapore-Batam data centre cluster most exposed to drought risk amid El Niño: BMI
article:
Scrutiny of water consumption by data centres is expected to intensify in 2027 amid heightened drought risk brought on by El Niño, according to BMI, a unit of data and analytics firm Fitch Solutions.

Around 17.6 gigawatts (GW), or 21%, of the 83.6GW data centre capacity tracked by BMI globally are in locations where El Niño raises water stress, the firm highlighted in a November outlook report on data centre sustainability.

Of that figure, 3.8GW of the capacity is live, with the remaining 13.8GW in the pipeline. Past El Niño cycles brought water shortages, rationing or emergency measures totalling 14.9GW to 16 locations, BMI added.

Drought and other El Niño-related risks are concentrated in Southeast Asia, with the Johor-Singapore-Batam cluster the most exposed, BMI said.

The cluster — which has some 6.6GW of capacity, including 4.7GW still in the pipeline — faces a higher risk of drought during an El Niño period.

BMI estimates that a drought occurred in 25% to 37% of El Niño-period months since 2013; in 2015, El Niño resulted in water levels in the Linggiu reservoir, which supplies both Johor and Singapore, to fall to record lows.

Data centre water consumption is already a hot-button issue in the two cities, which has prompted policymakers to respond, BMI’s report stated.

In Johor, approvals for water-intensive data centres have tightened since 2025, while Malaysia’s federal government said in October that states without sufficient water will not host data centres. In Batam, residents have protested against data centres over severe water shortages since August.

Against this backdrop, a dry spell in 2027 would test supply arrangements at the cluster’s 1.9GW of live capacity, and add to the risk of tighter permitting and cooling-technology requirements for the 4.7GW not yet built, BMI added.

Meanwhile, rising heat due to El Niño is expected to increase demand for water used to cool data centres, especially in Thailand, India and Indonesia.

“Above roughly 25°C, many data centres switch from outside-air to evaporative cooling, so water use rises with each extra degree,” the report said.

BMI estimates that 12.4GW of global data centre capacity faces above-average exposure to both drought and heat risks related to El Niño, with the most acute period likely being from late this year to 1H2027.

title: Manulife US Reit agrees on terms with lenders to exit restructuring, pending unitholder vote
article:
Manulife US REIT (MUST)  has negotiated a joint facilities agreement with its lenders that will allow it to exit its 2023 Master Restructuring Agreement (MRA).

The agreement marks “a significant step forward in MUST’s recovery and growth plans”, and brings the Reit closer towards the resumption of distributions to unitholders, the Reit’s manager said in a Nov 23 release. The Reit has haltered distributions to unitholders since 2023 as part of the restructuring.

The proposed agreement follows months of talks, which began “in earnest” after MUST completed divestments that achieved its minimum sale target of US$328.7 million as part of the MRA in June.

The agreement is contingent on the Reit’s unitholders passing three resolutions at an extraordinary general meeting to be held on Dec 15.

Among these are a resolution to renew a disposition mandate that will allow the manager to sell up to four of MUST’s existing proceeds to raise net proceeds not exceeding US$525 million (about $678 million).

The second resolution is for the renewal of an acquisition mandate that enables MUST to acquire industrial, living sector and retail assets in the US and Canada with an agreed property value capped at US$600 million.

The renewed disposition and acquisition mandates will give MUST more flexibility and time to sell properties, use the proceeds for deleveraging, and subsequently buying non-office assets, the manager said.

The third resolution is for a proposed trust deed amendment which gives the manager discretion to determine the level and frequency of distributions. Distributions will initially be capped at  the lower of 20% of annual distributable income of US$3 million a year, until all existing loans (including the sponsor-lender loan) are fully repaid or refinanced.

Under MUST’s deal with its lenders, the latter will grant loan maturity extensions of about 12 to 18 months each. The minimum bank interest coverage ratio will also be revised to 1.5 times, down from 2.0 times.

Other negotiated terms include the waiver of existing reinstatement conditions and the use of $28 million of MUST’s existing cash balance to partially repay loans due in 2027 and 2028.

As of Sept 30, MUST has reduced its total debt to US$487 million, down from US$1.03 billion in June 2023. Its leverage currently stands at 54%, with the manager targeting to reduce this to below 35% after full repayment of loans (excluding the sponsor-lender lo.

“We are now in the final stretch of a three-year journey, moving out from debt restructuring towards recovery and growth,” said John Cassante, CEO and chief investment officer of MUST’s manager.

He added: “Our priority is to resume distributions as soon as we can, with an aim of progressively increasing the payout after existing loans are fully repaid or refinanced, and as MUST achieves greater cash flow stability through diversification beyond office.”

title: Six city-centre shophouses linked to money laundering case up for sale at $109.8 mil
article:
A portfolio of six commercial shophouses in the city centre have been launched for sale by public tender, with a combined guide price of $109.75 million.

The properties comprise 77 Amoy Street; 28, 28A and 28B Keong Saik Road; 3 Stanley Street; 180 Telok Ayer Street; 198 Telok Ayer Street; and 534, 534A and 534B North Bridge Road .

The shophouses are among the non-cash assets forfeited in connection with Singapore’s $3 billion money laundering case, said Brilliance Capital, which is marketing the portfolio.

“Given the nature of the assets, the exercise will be conducted through a public tender, so that every prospective purchaser is assessed on the same terms and the outcome is fair and transparent,” added Sammi Lim, the firm’s founder and executive director, in a Nov 24 release.

Tenderers may submit bids for an individual property, a combination of properties, or for the portfolio as a whole. The individual properties are priced between $11 million and $29.4 million.

Summary of the properties

The largest property in the portfolio is a three-storey intermediate shophouse at 77 Amoy Street  which occupies a 999-year leasehold plot measuring 2,773 sq ft.  It has a gross floor area (GFA) of about 6,275 sq ft and is priced at $29.4 million, which translates to $4,685 psf.

The Keong Saik Road shophouse sits on a freehold 1,237 sq ft plot. The three-storey property with a mezzanine has a GFA of 3,025 sq ft. Its price: $14.2 million ($4,694 psf).

The property at 3 Stanley Street has a freehold land area of 1,310 sq ft. The three-storey shophouse, with an attic and a mezzanine, has a total GFA of 3,638 psf. Its guide price is $15.75 million ($4,329 psf).

The two Telok Ayer Street shophouses both have 999-year leasehold tenures. The shophouse at 180 Telok Ayer Street is a three-storey property with a roof mezzanine occupying a 1,644 sq ft site. Its guide price of $21 million translates to $4,724 psf on its 4,445 sq ft GFA.

Over at 198 Telok Ayer Street, the two-storey shophouse with an attic sits on a 1,654 sq ft plot. It is priced at $18.4 million, or $4,735 psf on its 3,886 sq ft GFA.

The North Bridge Road shophouse, spanning a land area of 880 sq ft, is a corner property with three storeys and an attic. The 999-year leasehold shophouse is priced at $11 million, translating to $3,488 psf on its GFA of 3,154 sq ft.

Brilliance Capital’s Lim noted that freehold and 999-year shophouses in the Telok Ayer and Keong Saik precincts are “rarely offered at the same time”.

She anticipates the tender to receive “keen interest” from a diverse range of buyers, including private investors, owner-occupiers, institutional funds and family offices.

The tender will close at 3pm on Jan 26, 2027.

title: Do You Sell When Your Small-Cap Grows into a Large-Cap?
article:
Every investor dreams of finding an overlooked
small-cap gem
and watching it blossom into a market giant.
Yet, when that dream actually comes true, it creates a surprising dilemma: should you take the money and run?
When you invest in a small company, you do so hoping to watch it expand.
Selling halfway along its journey simply because it outgrows its small-cap label makes little sense.
Why Did the Stock Cross S$1 Billion?
In Singapore, small-caps are typically defined as businesses with a market capitalisation under S$1 billion.
When one of your holdings crosses that threshold, your next move depends on why its value climbed.
Sometimes, a stock breaches the S$1 billion mark purely due to temporary market exuberance rather than underlying business progress.
When enthusiasm inflates a
valuation
beyond what is justified, you can simply sit tight and see if the share price settles back down.
On the other hand, if the company crossed S$1 billion because its operations genuinely expanded – and it has the potential to reach S$2 billion or more in the years ahead – you should let it keep running.
If you manage a dedicated small-cap portfolio and want to keep its focus pure, you do not have to hit the sell button.
Simply transfer that graduating stock into a separate portfolio without small-cap constraints, allowing it to keep compounding there.
Starting with one portfolio and eventually managing two because your winners outgrew the first is a wonderful problem to have.
Elephants, Fleas, and Growing Up
A common argument for selling is that elephants do not gallop, whereas fleas can jump thousands of times their own size.
Once a small company matures into a large-cap, its percentage growth rate naturally slows down.
Think of it like raising a child.
When a baby is born, they grow at an astonishing pace.
If you projected that infant growth rate forward indefinitely, you would assume you needed a ten-foot bed by the time they hit their teens.
Eventually, growth tapers off – not because anything is wrong, but because the child is maturing and developing new strengths.
Companies follow the exact same lifecycle.
Early on, revenue and profits surge rapidly.
As the business matures, growth moderates, yet the company often becomes more resilient and continues rewarding shareholders with
reliable dividends
.
While some investors prefer to cash out at S$1 billion to hunt for the next small-cap, holding on means keeping a proven, cash-generative business in your corner.
Get Smart: Conviction Beats Market Volatility
Outgrowing the small-cap label is a happy problem, not a reason to panic.
If you have done your homework and found a business capable of evolving into a market leader, you have already conquered the hardest part of investing – don’t discard a proven compounding machine just to chase an unproven gamble.

title: Can You Get More Than an 8% Dividend Yield from the Singapore Market?
article:
A portfolio offering more than an 8% dividend yield looks attractive on the surface but often raises red flags for experienced investors.
However, with the right strategy, it’s reasonably achievable with limited risks.
But how?
Here’s the hint: patience is key.
We examine a few scenarios patient investors can consider.
Scenario 1: Fully Invested in the Singapore Market
Real estate investment trusts
(REITs), including REIT exchange-traded funds (ETFs), have underperformed as debt taken on in the low-rate era is refinanced at
higher interest rates
.
Established REITs such as
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U) and
Frasers Centrepoint Trust
(SGX: J69U) currently offer distribution yields of more than 5%.
Investors who do not want to pick individual REITs can consider the
CSOP iEdge S-REIT Leaders Index ETF
(SGX: SRT), which has maintained a distribution yield of more than 5% since 2022.
Suppose you invest S$100,000 in these REITs and reinvest the distributions for the next 10 years. At a 5% yield, that’s a compounded return of 62.9%, growing your money to S$162,889.
Thereafter, a 5% distribution yield would give you about S$8,144 a year.
Based on your initial amount of S$100,000, that’s a yield on cost (YOC) of 8.1%.
This assumes unit prices and distributions stay flat over the 10 years. In reality, both can rise or fall.
Scenario 2: Fully Invested in the US Market – Locally
Four new
Xtrackers
ETFs were cross-listed on the
Singapore Exchange
(SGX: S68) on 13 October 2026.
Because these ETFs trade in Singapore dollars, you avoid upfront currency conversion fees. Splitting your money equally across all four would have given you an average annualised return of around 14% over the past 10 years, based on their underlying indices.
The caveat is that these returns may not repeat at the same rate in the future.

If you then move S$370,722 into Singapore holdings yielding 5% (as in Scenario 1), you would receive S$18,536 in annual dividends.
That’s a YOC of 18.5% based on your initial amount of S$100,000.
Scenario 3: 50/50 split between the Singapore and US markets
Can’t decide between the US and Singapore markets?
Why not simply allocate an equal amount to both?
Let’s see what the result looks like with the same initial capital of S$100,000.
If you put S$50,000 into the Xtrackers ETFs and it compounds at 14% per year, you would have about S$185,361 after 10 years.
The remaining S$50,000 is invested in Singapore holdings yielding 5%, with the dividends reinvested.
After 10 years, the Singapore portfolio would have grown to around S$81,445.
Together, the US and Singapore portfolios are now worth S$266,806.
If all the holdings are transferred to the Singapore market with a 5% dividend yield, that’s close to S$13,340 in annual dividends, or a YOC of 13.3% on your initial S$100,000.
Get Smart: Patient Investors Always Win
In all the above scenarios, there is only one common trait – that investors are willing to commit to their investment goals for at least 10 years, allowing time to do the heavy lifting.
That means delaying gratification and staying fully invested for the next decade, reinvesting every dividend along the way.
Simply by doing so, even in the conservative scenario of investing exclusively in the Singapore market, investors would still get an 8.1% YOC on their initial investment.
Patient investors win not because they are smarter, but because instead of timing the market, they maximise their time in the market.
While a 5% dividend yield is enough to achieve more than 8% YOC in the long run, it also helps to identify and invest in established dividend compounders that are more likely to increase their payouts regularly.
Young investors with time on their side may want to lean towards ETFs exposed to US equities, which offer higher growth opportunities.
With decades to invest, they can better tolerate the huge price swings typical of high-growth US equities.

title: OCBC Is Down 15%+ From Its High: What 100 Shares Pay You in Dividends
article:
Shares of
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, have
slipped well below
their September 2026 high.
If you own the bank for income, the better question is
what the shares pay you
.
Most of what OCBC paid you came as ordinary dividends, which rise and fall with the bank’s profit.
That profit is holding up, and the bank’s net interest income is growing again.
The special dividend is the part to question.
What did 100 OCBC shares pay you?
Over the past 12 months, OCBC paid S$1.05 per share in dividends.
On 100 shares, that comes to S$105.

Ordinary dividends make up S$89 of that S$105, or about 85%.
The S$16 special accounts for the rest.
Management has reaffirmed a 50% payout ratio for OCBC’s ordinary dividend.
In other words, the ordinary dividend moves with profit.
When profit grows, the ordinary dividend can grow with it.
Is the profit behind the ordinary dividend still growing?
For the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), OCBC’s net profit rose 3.2% year on year to S$2.04 billion.
It is only the
second time
the bank has earned more than S$2 billion in a quarter.
What about OCBC’s top line?
Total income fell 1.7% year on year to S$3.7 billion.
Net interest income (NII) rose 4% year on year to its highest level in six quarters.
The net interest margin (NIM), the gap between what OCBC earns on loans and investments and what it pays for funding, slipped 0.04 percentage points quarter on quarter to 1.66% in 3Q2026.
Higher US rates were the drag, as funding costs repriced faster than asset yields.
Management expects the margin to stabilise over the coming quarters.
Volume did the rest.
Net customer loans rose 13.7% year on year to S$367 billion.
For 2026 as a whole, OCBC expects NII to be flat to slightly lower.
Why did profit fall from 2Q2026’s record?
OCBC earned a record S$2.22 billion in 2Q2026.
The bank’s 3Q2026 profit came in 8% lower.
Great Eastern, OCBC’s insurance arm, accounted for much of the decline.
Its profit contribution to OCBC fell 69% quarter on quarter to S$147 million.
Great Eastern booked mark-to-market losses on its bonds, and its 2Q2026 equity gains did not repeat.
That pulled OCBC’s non-interest income down by nearly 10% year on year to S$1.42 billion.
The recurring business held up.
Net fees grew 8% year on year to S$735 million, with wealth management fees rising 2.6% to S$442 million.
Wealth management fees alone made up 11.8% of OCBC’s 3Q2026 total income.
Here’s the thing: Great Eastern’s investment income will swing with markets from quarter to quarter.
With a 50% payout ratio, those swings feed into your ordinary dividend.
What could squeeze the payout from here?
Start with the loan book.
New corporate non-performing assets (NPAs) fell to S$127 million in 3Q2026, down from S$300 million in 2Q2026.
OCBC also saw recoveries from some Greater China real estate accounts.
The non-performing loan (NPL) ratio improved to 0.8% from 0.9%, its first move since mid-2024.
AI lending is a new area of concern.
Data centres make up about 3% of OCBC’s loan book, and AI-related lending less than 1%.
Management said it only finances data centre projects that have secured power and an investment-grade hyperscaler, or large cloud computing company, to take up the capacity.
The S$16 special is the least certain part of your payout.
Management reaffirmed its plan to complete a S$2.5 billion capital return by the end of 2026.
Asked whether capital returns would extend into 2027, it said nothing had been announced.
Get Smart: Plan around the ordinary dividend
Before you count a bank’s dividend as income, split it into its ordinary and special parts.
Build your plans on the ordinary part, and treat anything extra as a bonus.
For OCBC, the next results will tell you more.
Check whether the ordinary dividend still tracks a 50% payout, and whether anything replaces the capital return after 2026.

What matters is where the extra cash came from.
A payout funded by rising profits can repeat, while one funded by a one-off gain or a timing quirk may not.
The three SGX stocks below all lifted their dividends by a third or more in their latest results.
Their reasons differ, and so do the odds of a repeat.

Is Tiong Woon’s bigger dividend backed by cash?
Tiong Woon Corporation Holding Ltd
(SGX: BQM) is an integrated heavy lift specialist.
For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), the board proposed a final dividend of S$0.025 per share, up from S$0.0175 a year ago – an increase of 43%.
Profits paid for it.
Revenue rose 15% year on year (YoY) to S$187.7 million, and profit attributable to shareholders climbed 24% to S$23.9 million.
Gross margin widened to 40.7% from 37.6% as the heavy lift segment earned higher margins.
Free cash flow is the lifeblood of dividends, and Tiong Woon’s improved sharply.
The group generated S$43.7 million in free cash flow, up from S$6.3 million.
Part of that improvement came from lower spending.
Cash spent on equipment fell 47%, yet total asset additions fell only 18%.
Over the same period, other secured borrowings rose to S$64.6 million from S$53.8 million.
The group carries S$108.0 million in debt against S$86.6 million in cash and bank deposits.
Management plans to keep renewing and expanding its fleet, so spending could climb again.
The dividend also grew faster than profit this year, but that gap cannot keep widening.
Can Boustead Singapore’s dividend outgrow a profit dip?
As Singapore’s
oldest continuous business organisation
,
Boustead Singapore Limited
(SGX: F9D) runs four divisions spanning real estate solutions, geospatial technology, energy engineering and healthcare.
For the six months ended 30 September 2026 (1HFY2027), the board declared an interim dividend of S$0.02 per share, 0.5 cents higher than a year ago.
That works out to an increase of 33%.
Reported profit moved the other way.
Revenue rose 38% YoY to S$406.6 million, while profit attributable to equity holders fell 10% to S$31.5 million.
Gross margin slipped to 32% from 38%, and a higher effective income tax rate weighed on earnings.
Boustead also booked an S$8.4 million reversal of its share of net asset value after opting out of a committed capital contribution to its associate, UIB Holdings; the move diluted its stake.
Adjusted for other gains and losses, impairments and other exceptional items, net profit rose 41% to S$39.5 million.
The order book offers support.
Real Estate Solutions revenue rose 83% to S$175.1 million, and the engineering order backlog stands at about S$720 million.
Its net liquid position reached S$313.0 million.
Geospatial is the part to watch.
Revenue there grew 26% to S$150.0 million, helped by the upfront recognition of most of its largest Enterprise Agreement renewal.
Boustead attributed this to the renewal’s licence terms, so the boost may not recur next half.
Why did Valuetronics double its interim dividend while profit fell?
Valuetronics Holdings Limited
(SGX: BN2) is an electronics manufacturing services provider.
For 1HFY2027, it declared an ordinary interim dividend of HK$0.08 per share, double the HK$0.04 paid a year ago.
Separately, it declared a special dividend of HK$0.06, up from HK$0.04.
The bigger payout follows a policy change.
In May 2026, Valuetronics raised its ordinary dividend target to 50% to 70% of net profit, from 30% to 50% previously, and set aside HK$300 million to return to shareholders over FY2027 and FY2028 through special dividends and share buybacks.
Revenue grew, but profit did not.
Revenue rose 7.3% YoY to HK$897.3 million as Industrial and Commercial Electronics (ICE) sales climbed 18.6% to HK$837.9 million.
Consumer Electronics revenue fell 54.3% to HK$59.4 million after the company phased out traditional consumer lifestyle products.
Profit attributable to owners declined 3.5% to HK$89.8 million.
Gross margin narrowed to 18.7% from 19.7% on higher component costs.
Income tax expense rose 50.9% after a Vietnam subsidiary moved from a full tax exemption to a 50% tax reduction.
Management expects ICE revenue to keep growing in FY2027, but that is subject to uncertainty over US trade and economic policies.
Still, the group expects to remain profitable.
A company that doubles its ordinary
dividend
while profit slips leaves itself less room for error.
That said, it held HK$1.15 billion in net cash as at 30 September 2026.
Get Smart: Sort the growth before you count it
A dividend increase is only as durable as its source.
Before you celebrate a higher payout, split it into two piles.
The first pile holds growth the business earned through higher profits and wider margins.
The second holds timing effects and one-offs, such as upfront revenue or a special dividend.
Tiong Woon’s increase sits mostly in the first pile, though its capex needs watching.
Boustead’s sits across both.
Valuetronics paid more while earning less.

title: US consumer confidence surges to highest since early 2025
article:
(Nov 24): US consumer confidence surged to the highest in nearly two years as Americans grew more optimistic about the economy and the job market.

The Conference Board’s gauge of confidence increased 11.4 points to 103.3 in November, the highest since January 2025, data released on Tuesday showed. That topped all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

A gauge of present conditions jumped 13.7 points to the highest since July 2025, while a measure of expectations for the next six months improved to the best since the end of 2024.

A broadly stable labour market paired with a weeks-long decline in gasoline prices likely supported confidence this month.

Confidence increased across all age groups but were largest among consumers with higher household incomes. Sentiment among Democrats and Independents improved sharply as Democrats saw sweeping victories in the latest midterm elections.

“Consumer confidence rallied again in November, potentially due to lower uncertainty following the midterm elections,” Fergus McCormick, a senior economist at the Conference Board, said in a statement. “While consumers continued to express frustration with high prices and rising costs, some comments cited hope for the general economy.”

See also: US consumer sentiment up on improved post-election utlook

In the lead up to the midterm elections, confidence fell in September to the lowest level in more than a decade as high food and energy bills ate into household budgets.

The latest report showed a greater share of consumers said business conditions were good and expect conditions to further improve in the months ahead. Similarly, Americans were more positive about the labor market now and in the future.

See also: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect more rate hikes

The Conference Board report showed the share of consumers that said jobs were plentiful rose to 30.8%, while the share saying jobs were hard to get decreased to 18.4%. The difference between the two — a metric closely followed by economists to gauge the job market — climbed to the widest since mid-2025.

There’s been early signs of momentum in the labour market, including strong hiring in October. A report from Glassdoor and Indeed showed a broadening in hiring demand across regions, with nearly half of US metro areas having more job postings in late September than a year earlier — the most since 2022.

The data aligns with the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index, which improved in November as gasoline prices fell and the outlook for business conditions improved.

The survey period for the report was Nov 1-17.

title: Boeing wins US$7.4 bil order in biggest China buy in years
article:
(Nov 24): Boeing Co received an order for 50 single-aisle jets from a subsidiary of China Southern Airlines Co, the country’s first major purchase from the US plane maker in years.

The order will consist entirely of 737-8 MAX planes, the subsidiary, Xiamen Airlines Co, said in an exchange filing on Tuesday, giving the country some much-needed new aircraft to update its ageing airliner fleets.

The list price of the 50 aircraft is valued at approximately US$7.4 billion, but the airline said that the final transaction price will be lower because of discounts provided by Boeing.

Boeing did not respond to a request for comment.

Following through on a vague commitment earlier this year by China to buy hundreds of Boeing aircraft, the order ends months of confusion that initially cast a pall over the planemaker’s return to the world’s second-largest aviation market.

On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he expected China to buy 250 more jets, which could bring the tally closer to the originally expected order for about 500 aircraft.

See also: Japan pledges financial support for International Criminal Court

Boeing, one of America’s largest exporters by dollar value, has been frozen out of China as it battled a string of production- and quality-related challenges, mostly stemming from major accidents. This deal marks Boeing’s biggest order from a Chinese airline since 2017.

Washington and Beijing have been locked in a long-running trade war, ranging from critical minerals to semiconductor chips. Trump has leveraged trade and used tariffs to secure favorable deals for American companies, and Boeing has been a major beneficiary.

For the past decade, China placed orders for several hundred Airbus SE aircraft, and its domestic airlines supplemented them by agreeing to buy hundreds of rival homegrown Commercial Aircraft Corp of China Ltd planes.

See also: How China and US clash over AI risks, robots and chip smuggling

Xiamen Air has a fleet of 174 aircraft, according to Planespotters.net, and also has several dozen planes on order, mostly from Airbus.

title: McCormick warns of ‘slippery slope’ after Trump pressured Nvidia to reinstate Huang
article:
(Nov 24): Republican Senator Dave McCormick warned that President Donald Trump’s intervention with the Nvidia Corp board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could create a “slippery slope”.

“I am worried about the precedent of the executive branch getting involved in really ownership deals with companies but also in board governance and making these decisions,” McCormick, the former chief of hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, told Bloomberg TV. “This is a precedent that I don’t think we want to replicate or reinforce.”

McCormick, who sidestepped questions about whether the Nvidia board erred in its decision to bring back Huang, will have the opportunity to question the embattled CEO next week when he testifies publicly before the Senate Banking Committee.

The Pennsylvania senator said he wants the panel to focus its questioning on whether any laws were broken, national security was compromised or Department of Commerce rules circumvented to get advanced chips into the hands of China.

“This also absolutely reinforces what I and a number of other members of the Senate have been saying, which is we need more legislation to restrict the export of these most advanced chips,” said McCormick, a former Commerce Department export control official. “I think this gives additional momentum to those legislative efforts.”

The comments are the latest sign that members of Trump’s own party are breaking with the president on his handling of China, artificial intelligence and Nvidia’s embattled leader.

See also: Lutnick under fire as Bessent blames Commerce Secretary in Nvidia crisis

US lawmakers are looking to attach export control provisions to the annual defence policy bill set for votes in the House and Senate in December. McCormick’s comments echo a Monday X post by Senate Intelligence chairman Tom Cotton, who said such provisions will be passed one way or another.

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bill,” Cotton said.

McCormick, when asked about Trump’s market involvement, also said he supports a ban on stock trading by elected officials. He warned that such measures will be needed to restore the public’s confidence in impartial decision-making by the government.

See also: Maga’s midterm defeat won’t change the course of history

McCormick’s wife, Dina Powell McCormick, is a top executive at Meta Platforms Inc and served as an adviser to Trump in his first term.

title: Forced buying aided biggest rally since April 2025, says Nomura
article:
(Nov 24): Wall Street roared back with its biggest rally since April 2025 on Monday, though analysis of the move suggests mechanical buying helped add momentum to the advance.

The S&P 500 Index jumped 4.7%, helped by Nvidia Corp’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he resigned. The news hit a market that had piled into protection during Friday’s tumble, which pushed the benchmark into correction territory.

As volatility collapsed on Monday, put options bought as hedges during the slide moved far out of the money, losing their sensitivity to the index, according to Charlie McElligott, a cross-asset strategist at Nomura Securities International Inc. Dealers who had sold futures against those puts had to buy them back, while short sellers rushed to cover their positions and investors chased the upside, he wrote in a note to clients on Monday. The Cboe Volatility Index fell more than nine points on the day.

The largest burst of buying was expected at the close. Leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) have to rebalance at the end of each session in the direction of the day’s move to keep their leverage constant. McElligott estimated these funds were on track to buy about US$41 billion — the second-largest daily buy in Nomura’s records.

That dwarfs the US$11 billion to US$16 billion of selling he projected from volatility-control funds, which cut exposure when market swings become too large.

See also: Subprime auto dealer America’s Car-Mart files for Chapter 11

More buying may now follow. Nomura’s model of trend-following funds, known as commodity trading advisers, had turned short on the S&P 500 across all time horizons in recent weeks. However, a close above 7,043 points for the index would be enough to flip the model’s 12-month signal back to a long, McElligott wrote. That would imply buying of about US$16 billion in S&P 500 futures and roughly US$2.5 billion for Nasdaq 100 contracts. The S&P 500 ended at 7,237.17 points on Monday, with futures on the back foot early Tuesday.

None of this settles the bigger concerns around the market, according to the Nomura strategist. He called it naive to think a one-day surge clears the catalysts behind the selloff, citing tighter financial conditions, a reset in assumptions on AI capital spending, inflation that remains too high, higher real rates and wider credit spreads.

“This ‘mechanical bounce’ guarantees us nothing with regard to those larger long-form ‘structural forces’,” he wrote in the note. But he added Huang’s return may preserve Nvidia’s role in financing the AI buildout, extending the cycle’s runway and reducing the risk of more severe outcomes.

title: Anthropic breaks below US$83 IPO price in premarket trading
article:
(Nov 24): Anthropic PBC shares traded below the US$83 IPO price in premarket trading, wiping out gains for investors who piled into the artificial intelligence lab’s record-setting debut.

The stock declined as much as 7.3% to US$81.28 per share as of 6.15am on Tuesday (Nov 24) in New York. The company's shares have been volatile, soaring briefly above US$100 on their first trading day following its initial public offering as investors cheered the arrival of a listed frontier AI firm.

Concerns over the pace of spending on the controversial technology roiled stocks even as bankers were working hard to lift the amount of money raised by the Claude chatbot maker’s debut above SpaceX’s record fundraise. Anthropic’s IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, with well over US$500 billion of demand translating into a US$119.5 billion haul for the company and its seven co-founders.

Anthropic’s IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, with allocations heavily skewed toward US-based investors, Bloomberg News reported. About 1,200 institutional investors placed orders, people familiar with the matter have said.

The rapid adoption of products such as Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding agent for software developers, and the company’s revenue run rate of US$81 billion at the end of October made for a powerful sales pitch. That helped investors overlook the company’s committed spending nearing US$901 billion through 2045.

SpaceX shares climbed as much as 67% above the IPO price before falling below it less than five weeks after its debut. A company’s shares sinking below that mark in the first few months of trading represents a blow to the narrative bankers have carefully constructed during the marketing. Some newly listed companies’ stock prices do not recover from breaching that important level.

See also: Zoom seeks Asia Pacific growth with AI beyond meetings

Anthropic and its rival OpenAI face mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, and the debate rages over whether the technology poses what Anthropic called “existential risks to humanity” in its IPO filing. OpenAI has filed confidentially for a listing but is not planning to go public before 2027.

title: Subprime auto dealer America’s Car-Mart files for Chapter 11
article:
(Nov 24): America’s Car-Mart Inc, a used-car seller and subprime lender, filed for bankruptcy to sell the business under court supervision.

The Rogers, Arkansas-based company filed for Chapter 11 in the Southern District of Texas on Tuesday, court documents showed. It listed assets of US$100 million to US$500 million and liabilities of US$1 billion to US$10 billion in its petition.

America’s Car-Mart is one of the best known in the “buy here, pay here” segment of auto finance, where companies operate their own dealerships and provide financing to customers in-house. The sector caters to “deep” subprime borrowers who often can’t obtain financing elsewhere.

Once a market darling of the Covid pandemic era, the cash-strapped company has come under pressure after interest rate hikes put an end to ultra-cheap borrowing. In June, America’s Car-Mart defaulted on a US$300 million term loan from Silver Point Capital to repay its asset-backed line of credit and had been operating under short-dated forbearance extensions. It listed total debts of US$624 million in its earnings report for the first quarter that ended July 31.

The company has struggled to emerge from its performance rut, constrained by reduced inventory and limited capacity to write new loans. It reported revenue of US$146 million in the first quarter, a 57% plunge from the year-ago period. Meanwhile, the value of its inventory fell 35% from the prior three months, as the company curtailed new purchases and sold its vehicles in order to preserve liquidity.

title: LME to list major new aluminium brand as historic squeeze deepens
article:
(Nov 24): The London Metal Exchange is preparing to authorise deliveries of aluminium from a major new smelter in Indonesia into its warehousing network, offering potential supply relief as a historic squeeze roils the global market.

The LME is in the final stages of authorising metal produced by PT Hua Chin Aluminium Indonesia for delivery against its contracts, following on from its brand application in May, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the registration is still being finalised.

Hua Chin is one of several new smelters being built and ramped up in Indonesia, and the 480,000-tonne-a-year plant could help to alleviate inventory shortages and pricing pressures on the LME that have exposed the global aluminium industry to heavy losses.

Spot aluminium prices on the LME have traded at huge premiums to later-dated futures over recent days, moving into the biggest backwardation since an infamous squeeze in the 1980s. The ructions have come as LME inventories have slumped to the lowest level since 1990, with surging output in Indonesia bringing little relief so far because only one of the country’s smelters produces LME-deliverable metal.

title: Ex-RBI chief Rajan sees Nvidia governance risk with return of Huang
article:
(Nov 24): Jensen Huang’s surprise return to lead Nvidia Corp puts a spotlight on corporate governance and the company’s pivotal role in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, according to former Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Raghuram Rajan.

Rajan, a finance professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, said the global rally that followed also raised questions about the US government’s role in putting him back in charge, and governance at Nvidia under his renewed leadership.

“Are there going to be checks and balances on him?” Rajan said in an interview with Bloomberg Television’s Haslinda Amin. He asked whether potential malfeasance would be thoroughly investigated by the US chipmaker.

Huang’s return to the company at the centre of the AI boom restored confidence in technology stocks after his exit earlier this month rattled the trade. But Rajan said a larger question that predated the latest turmoil remains: whether returns on trillions of dollars of investment in computing can justify the debt-fuelled spending.

Rajan said some people compare Nvidia to American International Group Inc during the 2008 global financial crisis because it sits at the centre of many contracts and helps keep the boom going. He said the systemic risk isn’t significant now but could grow given the scale of planned investment.

Rajan stopped short of calling AI a bubble, saying it may simply reflect excessive optimism. He said security concerns, particularly in the event of a major cyberattack, could trigger a sharp drop in demand.

See also: Australia bolsters online safety law with tougher Big Tech fine

title: German business outlook improves for seventh straight month
article:
(Nov 24): Germany’s business outlook improved for a seventh month, cementing hopes that the economy has finally overcome years of stagnation.

An expectations index by the Ifo institute rose to 91.9 in November from a revised 91.5 the previous month, almost matching the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey of 92. A measure of current conditions also advanced.

“The recovery of the German economy is proceeding, but it lacks breadth,” Ifo president Clemens Fuest said on Tuesday in a statement that described improvements for services and trade, while manufacturing and construction suffered setbacks.

Europe’s biggest economy has performed much more strongly than expected when the Iran war broke out in February. Large-scale government spending is providing a tailwind, as are exports, underpinned by the investment boom in artificial intelligence.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s economic advisers have more than doubled their forecast for GDP growth to 1.3% this year and 1% in 2027. Such optimism has been backed up by indicators including S&P Global’s Purchasing Managers Index, which unexpectedly surged to its highest level in more than four and a half years in November.

See also: Australia to lower nominal economy estimate in budget update

Inflation remains a concern, with the Bundesbank predicting price gains will pick up at the start of 2027 as a temporary fuel rebate expires. There’s also concern that low gas-storage levels could lead to a price spike in case of a cold winter.

Elsewhere, the European Central Bank is set to raise interest rates for the third time this year in December, taking them into territory where they may act as a brake on growth. Some policymakers have said further tightening is possible.

title: China extends pause on US minerals ban to maintain truce
article:
(Nov 24): China extended the suspension of a ban on exports of several critical minerals to the US, preserving a key element of a fragile trade truce despite growing tensions over technology.

China’s Commerce Ministry on Tuesday kept the ban on US-bound shipments of gallium, germanium and antimony on hold through Jan 27, prolonging a suspension that was due to expire Friday. The materials are used in products ranging from semiconductors to satellites and military equipment.

The extension follows last week’s summit between Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping in Shenzhen and comes hours after the US president helped secure the reinstatement of Jensen Huang, a vocal opponent to stringent chip export controls, as the chief of Nvidia Corp on Monday.

But Washington has also tightened restrictions on China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centres. If fully enforced, the measures could hamper Beijing’s efforts to catch up with the US in AI.

The US Commerce Department announced the new rules just days before the summit. China’s Commerce Ministry said the restrictions violated understandings reached by the two leaders and warned of countermeasures if Washington presses ahead.

China first imposed the US-specific critical minerals ban in December 2024 in retaliation against the Biden administration’s widening chip curbs. It suspended its enforcement last November after Trump and Xi struck a trade truce in South Korea, setting Nov 27, 2026, as the expiration date.

See also: China stockpiles soyoil as domestic prices hit three-month low

The extension brings the suspension into line with other elements of the truce that run through January, including tariff relief and a pause on additional Chinese export controls on rare earths that are set to expire on Jan 10.

China’s dominance of critical mineral supply chains proved a powerful source of leverage in last year’s trade war, when Beijing’s export controls helped pressure Washington to back down.

China accounts for 99% of global production of primary low-purity gallium, about 80% of natural graphite output, and 36% of mined antimony, according to US Geological Survey estimates for 2025. The agency also identified China as the leading global producer and exporter of germanium metal in 2025, without specify its share.

title: JPMorgan and HSBC trade digital gold in London for first time
article:
(Nov 24): JPMorgan Chase & Co and other major precious metals dealers traded a new form of digital gold in London for the first time, an early test of a system that could revamp the plumbing of the world’s biggest bullion hub.

JPMorgan, HSBC Holdings plc and StoneX Group Inc completed their first trades using fractional ownership interests in physical gold bars last week, the World Gold Council industry group said in a statement. While still at a trial stage, a successful rollout of the new system could mark one of the most significant additions to the structure of the London bullion market in decades.

“This is a historic step forward for the gold market,” said David Tait, chief executive officer of the WGC, which led the initiative. “For the first time, leading institutions have transferred, settled and used fractional ownership of physical gold as collateral through real, live transactions.”

Hundreds of billions of dollars worth of gold change hands every week in London, setting benchmark prices for the global precious metals industry. What is traded in that market, for the most part, are “unallocated” paper contracts that oblige the vaulting bank to deliver gold on request.

Trading unallocated gold is cheaper and easier than transacting in hefty 400 ounce bars, allowing traders to pay lower storage fees and deal in precise quantities of metal. The drawbacks are that holders remain exposed to the creditworthiness of the vaulting bank, and that the paper claims cannot generally be used as collateral.

See also: Gold extends gain after Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang sparks rally

Banks can post the new fractional gold — called ‘pooled gold interests’ — as collateral without needing to move the physical metal, potentially making bullion a more useful financial asset. The WGC is also lobbying UK authorities to bring gold within the country’s financial-collateral regime, which would make it easier to pledge and enforce in insolvency.

Gold that is fractional, easily transferable and shielded from the insolvency of an intermediary would allow the metal “to be used more widely across financial markets, including as collateral”, Mark Amlin, global head of physical commodities at JPMorgan, said in the statement.

Asian financial centres are looking to capture a greater share of bullion trading from London. Hong Kong began trial operations of a new gold clearing system similar to London’s this year, while Singapore unveiled measures including a gold vaulting service for central banks.

See also: Gold rebounds as tech rout spurs shift to havens, Treasury rally

Earlier this year, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority sought the views of the financial sector on gold tokenization, adding that developing the next generation of gold-market infrastructure would “reinforce and preserve London’s position as a centre for gold trading and custody”.

With well over US$1 trillion ($1.29 trillion) worth of gold in its vaults, including mounds of central bank-owned metal underneath the Bank of England, London is unlikely to lose its position as the dominant trading hub anytime soon. Many traders also expect the market will probably maintain its primarily “unallocated” structure, even if pooled gold interests prove to be popular with dealers and clients.

Not all prior attempts to reform London’s precious metals market have been successful. Four years ago, the London Metal Exchange abandoned an effort to move more trading onto an exchange, an initiative backed by banks including Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley, after the contracts failed to attract sufficient volumes.

Unlike some previous attempts to reshape London’s bullion market, pooled gold interests are designed to work alongside the existing over-the-counter system, rather than shift trading away from it, said Mike Oswin, global head of market structure at the WGC. “We are not here to say the unallocated market isn’t working,” Oswin said. “This is complementary to it.”

Several elements still need to be worked out before pooled gold interests can be rolled out more broadly, he added, including deciding how the system would be governed.

Five banks currently provide vaulting and oversee the existing clearing infrastructure in the London market: Citigroup Inc, ICBC Standard Bank, UBS Group AG, HSBC, and the biggest player, JPMorgan. Deutsche Bank AG and Morgan Stanley are also seeking to join the small club, Bloomberg reported in October.

title: Japan pledges financial support for International Criminal Court
article:
(Nov 24): Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to continue supporting the International Criminal Court and ICC President Tomoko Akane as the organisation and its Japanese leader come under increasing pressure from the US and Russia.

“I received the very welcome news that a decision has been made to pay Japan’s full 2027 contribution to the ICC within the current year. I understand that this initiative was personally spearheaded by the prime minister,” Akane said to reporters after meeting with Takaichi on Tuesday (Nov 24).

Japan’s foreign ministry confirmed that Takaichi said Tokyo would accept a request for early payment of Tokyo’s contribution to the operations of the ICC for next year.

Akane has been sanctioned by the US as part of an offensive against the ICC for allegedly unfairly targeting the US and Israel in its investigation into the conflict in Gaza. She is also on Russia’s wanted list along with other officials over the court’s 2023 arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Takaichi told Akane that Japan would continue to “strongly support the ICC and President Akane in order to enable the ICC to fulfil its role and functions as originally envisaged,” according to the foreign ministry statement.

The ICC was singled out in a short statement following a meeting between Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping held last week, at which they “agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”.

See also: How China and US clash over AI risks, robots and chip smuggling

For Takaichi, differences over the ICC represent a rare public point of friction between Japan and the US. She has said Japan would continue to provide support to Akane, who is now barred from the US financial system and travel to the US, and would consider making further representations to the US as appropriate.

“The prime minister said that Japan will continue to provide robust support for international organisations, including the ICC, just as it has done in the past. Furthermore, she emphasised a commitment to upholding the rule of law and working in cooperation with neighbouring and other relevant nations to promote this principle,” Akane said after her meeting with Takaichi.

ICC judges have issued a total of 68 arrest warrants, according to its website, including one against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2024 for alleged war crimes in Gaza and another for Putin in 2023 over war crimes related to the alleged abduction of children from Ukraine. Trump imposed fresh sanctions on the organisation in October, the same day that a former ICC judge won the Nobel Peace Prize.

See also: World War II still has lessons for today’s wars

Tokyo is the largest financial backer of the court. “As the largest financial contributor to the ICC, we must protect this important institution,” Takaichi said in August after the US move to sanction Akane.

title: Australia bolsters online safety law with tougher Big Tech fine
article:
(Nov 24): The world’s biggest technology providers may face fines of as much as 5% of their global revenue under Australia’s new Digital Duty of Care law after the government toughened penalties to secure its passage.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said Tuesday the bill will pass parliament this week after its amendments won the support of the minority Greens party. The maximum penalty for breaching the law was raised from a previously proposed ceiling of A$109 million (US$72 million or $141 million).

The sweeping legislation seeks to reduce online harm by compelling digital service providers from social media platforms to AI chatbots to build safety into their products. It will also allow social media users to switch off algorithms that determine what content they see.

Australians would also be able to sue companies for harm caused by breaches of the law. Wells described the legislation as Australia’s most significant step yet to improve online safety.

Wells said in an interview last month that she wants to use the legislation as a step towards working with other countries and establish basic online safety standards, particularly for children.

title: Japan’s Fujitsu woos demand for alternatives to US, China chips
article:
(Nov 24): Initial demand for Fujitsu Ltd’s new Monaka server chips is exceeding expectations, fuelled by clients seeking alternatives to US and Chinese suppliers, according to the company’s chief technology officer.

Shortly after the Tokyo-based company began commercial sales of its latest 2nm central processing units this month, Fujitsu already is in discussions with its manufacturer Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co about securing enough production capacity, Vivek Mahajan said.

Demand for sovereign data security in areas including defence, finance, manufacturing and the public sector is boosting interest from customers in Japan, the US and Europe, he said.

“The biggest challenge is — if the demand really takes off, can we make sure that the supply keeps up?” Mahajan said in an interview on Tuesday (Nov 24). Most of the 45 companies that received Monaka product samples in August are likely to place orders, he said.

The Fujitsu-Monaka processors — named after a traditional Japanese confectionary — may face supply constraints if orders exceed the company’s current topline estimates of sales of about 500,000 units over two years, Mahajan said. A single manufacturer shipping about 30,000 servers would need more than 200,000 Monaka chips, he said.

Fujitsu, which supplies the Japanese government computing, artificial intelligence, networking and security products, has mostly restricted use of its processors to its own systems, such as for use in the Fugaku supercomputer. With Monaka, Fujitsu seeks to sell its processors — which use Arm Holdings plc architecture — to other server makers and turn the business into a new revenue driver.

See also: Jensen Huang to brief US Congress on affair following Nvidia ouster

Fujitsu expects Monaka chips to generate ¥35 billion in sales in the next fiscal year, with annual sales reaching ¥500 billion by 2035. Fujitsu may hit the longer-term target a couple years earlier, Mahajan said. Analysts on average expect Fujitsu’s revenue to stay flat this fiscal year to March at ¥3.6 trillion and for the company to clock about 5% growth each year through 2030.

AI data centres need more CPUs to deal with the rising volume of everyday tasks and general-purpose computing that users now demand of agents. Intel Corp and Advanced Micro Devices Inc now dominate the server CPU market but the two face pressure from Arm-based chips as well as from Nvidia Corp, which touts energy efficiency.

Monaka is targeting companies and governments’ need for better performance, memory access and security as well as energy efficiency, Mahajan said.

See also: New US export controls on Singapore, Malaysia for advanced chips to take effect Nov 19

“We are the only ones in Japan that make a CPU today and probably only ones outside the US that make such a cutting-edge CPU,” he said. “That’s an alternative that we give to our customers.”

title: Singapore, China deepen yuan ties with focus on corporates
article:
(Nov 24): The central banks of Singapore and China will expand ways for financial institutions to access yuan funding in the city-state to help finance a broader range of corporate activities, in another step to promote the currency’s international use.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the People’s Bank of China will upgrade the MAS RMB Facility to better meet the growing yuan financing needs in the region, according to a statement Monday. The facility, backed by a bilateral currency swap deal, will be structured into two parts: an RMB Corporate Facility and an RMB Liquidity Facility.

The deal with Singapore aligns with broader efforts by the PBOC’s Shanghai branch to expand the yuan’s role as a pricing, investment and reserve currency over the next decade, including supporting multinational corporations in conducting global treasury management in yuan and developing offshore markets.

“This latest initiative reinforces Singapore’s position as one of the leading offshore RMB hubs, especially being a gateway for Southeast Asia,” said Frances Cheung, head of foreign exchange and rates strategy at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “The enhanced facilities will promote the use of RMB in a broad range of transactions such as trade financing, working capital and intra-group funding.”

The corporate facility will fund third-country trade financing, working capital, capital expenditure and eligible intra-group transactions in yuan, with borrowing tenors expanding up to six months, MAS said. The liquidity facility will continue to provide backstop funding to support stability in Singapore’s offshore yuan market.

See also: Dollar heads for fourth week of gains following Anthropic IPO

The move comes as yuan deposits in Singapore reached a record high of 337 billion yuan (US$50.6 billion or $65.3 billion) at the end of the first half of 2026, according to MAS data compiled by Bloomberg. The initiatives were announced at a Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation meeting in Singapore on Monday.

The corporate and liquidity facilities are backed by a bilateral currency swap arrangement of up to 300 billion yuan and $65 billion, which MAS and the PBOC renewed in 2022 through 2027. The facilities will accept Singapore Government Securities and MAS Bills as collateral alongside local-dollar cash, with Chinese government bonds also under consideration, according to the MAS statement.

“If China government bonds become eligible collateral, this would help further increase the incentives for investors to hold Chinese bonds,” Cheung said.

See also: China sets strongest yuan fixing since 2022 as Apec begins

Beyond these facilities, MAS and the PBOC are exploring linking their fast-payment systems for small-value transfers, according to the statement. MAS and the China Securities Regulatory Commission also pledged to support cross-border corporate listings and new exchange-traded funds with the Shanghai and Shenzhen bourses.

title: South Korea considers potential US$3 bil dollar bond sale
article:
(Nov 24): South Korea is considering issuing potentially about US$3 billion of dollar-denominated notes in January.

The government sent out requests for proposals for the possible offering earlier this month and is receiving presentations from banks this week to select arrangers, according to a finance ministry official. Details of the sale may change depending on market conditions.

The start of the new calendar year is typically one of the busiest periods for global primary markets, and the offering would be part of the government’s regular issuance of offshore debt to bolster foreign-exchange reserves to act as a buffer during periods of volatility. The government is seeking parliamentary approval to issue as much as US$8 billion of such bonds in 2027.

Both China and Indonesia have already tapped the dollar bond market this month, preferring to lock in funds while they can, despite elevated volatility in financial markets. South Korea last sold US$3 billion in dollar bonds in February of 2026.

The won’s wild swings this year underscore the desire of authorities to maintain ample firepower against fresh market volatility. The currency has rallied more than 16% against the US currency since hitting a 17-year low in June, as exporters led by chipmakers stepped up sales of dollars to fund projects at home.

That rally marks a dramatic turnaround after the won was Asia’s worst performer against the greenback in the first half.

See also: Rakuten Group shelves bond sale of up to ¥151 bil

The Bank of Korea’s foreign currency reserves stood at about US$443 billion at the end of October, the highest level since May 2022, according to central bank data.

title: Japan LNG buying poised to rise as gas power turns profitable
article:
(Nov 24): Japan is poised to buy more liquefied natural gas (LNG) in the spot market as improving economics for gas-fired power generation boost the fuel’s appeal after months of favouring coal.

The so-called physical spark spread — which measures the profitability of using spot LNG to generate electricity — turned positive on a seven-day average for the first time since the Iran war began in late February, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That means utilities can earn a margin buying LNG, burning it for power, and selling the electricity.

The shift is largely a result of higher spot power prices, with day-ahead prices on the Japan Electricity Power Exchange hitting successive peaks not seen in more than four years. The nationwide spot price climbed to ¥37.5 (24 cents) a kilowatt-hour on Monday, the highest since August 2022.

If this trend continues, utilities will be incentivised to turn increasingly to spot LNG in place of coal, according to traders. Any pickup in purchases from Japan — one of the world’s biggest importers — could drive prices in Asia higher and tighten an already-strained global market as the Northern Hemisphere heads into winter.

Japan’s recent preference for cheaper coal has contributed to a 9% year-on-year decline in the 30-day moving average for LNG deliveries to the country, according to ship-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg.

See also: Chinese refiners snapping up cut-price oil to refill stockpiles

If the country seeks more spot LNG, it would also be competing with European buyers for the same supply at a time when the continent is grappling with low inventories and falling temperatures. Gas prices in Europe jumped this week after forecasts showed colder conditions persisting across parts of the region.

Temperatures have also begun to fall in Japan, signalling the onset of winter. That’s likely to reinforce spot power market prices into January and February, when the country’s seasonal power demand typically peaks.

title: India banking cash turns to deficit, first time since June
article:
(Nov 24): India’s banking-system liquidity slipped into deficit for the first time in about five months, as recent tax outflows drained cash from lenders.

Banks borrowed a net of 128.25 billion rupees from the Reserve Bank of India as of Nov 21, the first such occurrence since June 29, according to RBI data. Net borrowing from the central bank indicates deficit liquidity conditions.

Banking-system liquidity has fallen since hitting a record surplus in September, when foreign-exchange inflows under the RBI’s capital-raising programme to support the rupee flooded lenders with cash. The central bank has since absorbed excess cash through its operations, including bond sales and FX swaps.

Goods and services tax payments were the latest trigger for the move into deficit, according to IDFC First Bank. When individuals and companies pay taxes, the funds are transferred to a government account that is held separately from their bank accounts by the RBI, reducing liquidity available in the banking system.

“Going forward, the key drain will be currency leakage, which picks up in the October-to-March period and has shown a significant surge this year,” said Gaura Sen Gupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank in Mumbai, referring to cash withdrawals from banks. The liquidity deficit may persist into the next quarter, she said.

See also: India’s new data series to aid RBI policy, Gupta says

The cash crunch has pushed banks’ overnight borrowing costs above the RBI’s policy rate. The so-called weighted average call rate was about 25 basis points above the RBI’s 5.5% benchmark on Monday. The call rate, which is the price at which banks lend funds to each other, is typically anchored to the policy rate.

Higher overnight funding costs for banks typically push up yields on shorter-maturity bonds too, raising borrowing costs across the economy and potentially weighing on growth. India’s five-year yields climbed five basis points on Monday to 6.99%.

To ease the immediate crunch, the central bank undertook two rounds of cash injections on Monday, providing lenders with a total of 1 trillion rupees through transactions that reverse in the coming days. Indian markets are shut Tuesday (Nov 24) for a holiday.

title: Chinese refiners snapping up cut-price oil to refill stockpiles
article:
(Nov 24): Chinese state-owned and independent refiners have boosted oil purchases this month, taking advantage of falling crude and transport costs to replenish stockpiles depleted by the Middle East war.

Unipec — the trading arm of China’s biggest refiner Sinopec — has bought as many as 20 cargoes, usually of about one million barrels each, from West Africa for December loading, according to traders. That compares with a monthly average of roughly 20 million to 25 million barrels from the region to all of China.

The Chinese buyers are also snapping up Persian Gulf and Brazilian shipments. Prompt Saudi and Iraqi barrels have been changing hands at US$2 to US$3 a barrel above the Dubai benchmark on a delivered basis to East Asia, said the traders, asking not to be named as they are not authorised to speak to media. That is down from US$12 for Basrah crude a month ago.

The wave of buying comes as the global oil market is forecast to return to surplus next year, with the help of a recovery in Persian Gulf exports despite the still unresolved conflict. Global benchmark Brent has plunged by around a quarter so far in November, and a key question is whether the Chinese purchases will be enough to arrest the slide.

As crude prices came down, “the most noticeable tranche of incremental buying is from China,” said June Goh, an analyst at Sparta Commodities SA. “That’s because others like the Japanese and South Koreans were already buying at maximum levels over the last few months.”

See also: Indonesia says recent Singapore gas cuts due to pipeline repairs

The falling cost of freight is also helping to spur the buying activity. The cost of shipping a barrel of crude from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to around US$8 a barrel, down from about US$21 last month. Vessel earnings for most major routes to Asia have also dropped.

title: Intesa opens US$36 bil bid on world’s oldest bank to investors
article:
(Nov 24): Intesa Sanpaolo SpA is submitting its €33 billion (US$36 billion) takeover offer for Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena SpA to investors, starting a process that could end independence for the world’s oldest bank.

Monte Paschi shareholders can start tendering their stock on Tuesday and the last day is Jan 22. Intesa has set an acceptance threshold of two-thirds but it has left the door open to cutting that to 50%.

If Intesa chief executive officer Carlo Messina prevails, Italy’s largest bank will take ownership of a bank founded as a pawn agency in 1472 during the Italian Renaissance. More recently, the bank became a symbol for scandal and mismanagement before recovering thanks to various state bailouts, capital injections and ultimately a turnaround under CEO Luigi Lovaglio.

The deal would cement Intesa’s position as Italy’s dominant lender and hand it wealth-management operations overseeing close to €2 trillion in client financial assets. Messina has pledged to sell parts of Monte Paschi’s operations to insurer Unipol to address potential competition concerns.

Messina has tailwind going into the acceptance period as several Monte Paschi investors have already indicated support for the offer. That includes the biggest shareholder, the Del Vecchio family’s holding company Delfin Sarl. Still, Intesa needs broader backing to get the transaction over the line.

Monte Paschi itself hasn’t taken a clear stance on the matter, with the board over the weekend saying Intesa’s bid is “fair” but doesn’t “fully reflect” its value. Independent director Corrado Passera resigned during the board meeting discussing the assessment, highlighting differing opinions on the governance body.

See also: Coca-Cola HBC rises in JSE debut ahead of US$2.6 bil deal

Intesa is offering €1.25 in cash and 1.664 newly issued shares for each Monte Paschi share, valuing the target at about €33 billion at Monday’s close. Intesa may choose to opt for an extension of the acceptance period lasting from Feb 1 through Feb 5.

Monte Paschi owns about 86% of Mediobanca, meaning a takeover would require Intesa to make an offer for the firm’s listed shares, at an estimated cost of €2.8 billion. Mediobanca in turn owns roughly 13% of Assicurazioni Generali SpA, Italy’s largest insurer.

title: Indonesia says recent Singapore gas cuts due to pipeline repairs
article:
